title: Advanced Computer Skills and Abattoir Management Information

lessons.title: Management information in an abattoir
lessons.html:
From data to decisions

Data are raw facts: a carcass mass, a temperature, a clock-in time. Information is data that has been organised so it means something: the average dressing percentage per supplier this month, or how many hours chiller 2 was above its limit. A management information system (MIS) collects data, processes it and presents information that managers use to make decisions.

Data sources in an abattoir

SourceData
ReceivingSupplier, numbers, live mass, movement document numbers
Slaughter and weighing systemCarcass number, hot mass, classification, owner
Inspection recordsCondemnations by cause and part
Temperature loggersChiller, freezer and vehicle temperatures
Time and attendanceHours, overtime, absence
Maintenance logsDowntime, causes, repair times
Sales and dispatchCustomers, products, quantities, prices

Good information is

  • Accurate: built on correct data entry.
  • Timely: available when the decision must be made.
  • Relevant: answers the question the manager has.
  • Clear: easy to read, using tables and charts.
  • Comparable: uses the same definitions each period so trends are real.

Rubbish in, rubbish out: if workers enter wrong lot numbers, every report built on that data is wrong. The foreman is responsible for data quality from the floor.

lessons.title: Advanced spreadsheet skills
lessons.html:
Working with larger data sets

Data exported from the abattoir system usually comes as a spreadsheet with one row per carcass or per event. Advanced skills let you turn thousands of rows into useful reports.

Useful functions

  • SUMIF / COUNTIF: add or count only rows that meet a condition. Example: =COUNTIF(D:D,"Fluke") counts livers condemned for fluke.
  • AVERAGEIF: average for one group, for example dressing percentage for one supplier.
  • IF: test a condition, for example =IF(E2>7,"Check","OK") to flag a temperature reading above a limit stored as 7 in your procedure.
  • VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP: look up information from another table, such as supplier names from a supplier code.
  • ROUND: round results to sensible decimals.

Sorting and filtering

Sort data by date, supplier or value. Filters let you show only the rows you need, such as all detained carcasses this week.

Pivot tables

A pivot table summarises large data quickly, for example total carcass mass and number of condemnations per supplier per month, without writing formulas. Change the layout by dragging fields.

Charts

  • Line charts for trends over time, such as weekly yield.
  • Bar charts for comparisons, such as condemnation rates per supplier.
  • Keep charts simple: clear title, labelled axes, few colours.

Protecting the data

Keep the original export unchanged and work on a copy. Lock formula cells if others use the sheet. Check totals against the source system so you know the report is correct.

lessons.title: Reports, dashboards and data security
lessons.html:
Writing management reports

A good management report answers: what happened, why, and what we are doing about it.

  1. Summary: three to five key messages at the top.
  2. Key performance indicators: actual versus target and versus last period, such as throughput, yield, condemnations, hygiene results, overtime and injuries.
  3. Exceptions: anything outside its limit, with the cause.
  4. Actions: what has been done or is planned, by whom and by when.

Dashboards

A dashboard shows a few key indicators on one screen or page, often with traffic-light colours: green on target, amber at risk, red off target. Dashboards help a foreman spot problems at a glance, but always look at the underlying data before acting.

Using information to improve

Example: a pivot table shows that one supplier's lots have twice the bruising trim of others. Further analysis shows the problem is linked to one transporter. The foreman shares the data with procurement, who discuss loading and transport with the supplier. Bruising drops the next month. This is information turning into action.

Data security and privacy

  • Control who can view and change data, using user accounts and permissions.
  • Back up data regularly and test that backups can be restored.
  • Protect personal information of workers and suppliers as required by the Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013.
  • Do not e-mail sensitive spreadsheets to personal accounts.
  • Use strong passwords and watch for phishing e-mails asking for login details.

Key points

  • Data are raw facts; information is organised data that supports decisions.
  • Accurate data entry on the floor is the foundation of every report.
  • Use COUNTIF, SUMIF, lookups and pivot tables to summarise large data.
  • Reports should show what happened, why, and the actions planned.
  • Control access, back up data and protect personal information.
